newsitem.title: INDIA: Indian coffee exporters cancel forward contracts.
newsitem.headline: Indian coffee exporters cancel forward contracts.

text.p: Indian coffee exporters are cancelling forward contracts amid fears that the government might impose export controls due to a shortfall in domestic stocks, traders said on Wednesday.

They said exporters were keen to cancel contracts as prices in the domestic market were expected to rise above global prices and feared that the government would clamp down on exports to ensure a steady supply in the local market in the winter months.
"All export contracts between September and December have been cancelled. These stocks will be made available in the domestic market," said Ashwin Shah, a leading exporter.

Traders did not give details about the quantity of coffee on forward contracts being cancelled. But they said that while some exporters had already cancelled contracts, many more were in the process of doing so.
India exports about 180,000 tonnes of coffeea year.
Forward contracts -- agreements entered into by an exporter to export at a specified date and at a certain price -- generally contain provisions for cancellation.
But if exporters cancel a forward contract, they have to pay a damage cost or penalty, Coffee Board officials said. It is not legally binding. Legal provisions are only for the payment of penalty.

Coffee Board chairman Philipose Matthai said that in the event of a shortage, the government had several options including capping exports, allowing imports, and purchase of coffee by the board from growers for further sales.
Shah said exporters would be able to make up the loss suffered on forward contracts since domestic rates were higher than world prices.
Traders said the domestic price of coffee was about 120 rupees per kg, compared to 80 rupees in the global market.
Commerce Minister B.B. Ramaiah said last week that the government would not tolerate a speculative price rise in the doemstic market following the abolition of a quota system.
He said the government would encourage imports if necessary.
The government announced on September 14 that coffee growers would no longer be required to pool their output for auction by the state-run Coffee Board in domestic and export markets.
It abolished a quota system that obligated growers to sell 30 percent of their output to the pool.
Dealers said coffee powder prices in the retail market rose five to ten rupees per kg following the government decision.
They predicted a further increase of about 15 rupees per kg by the year-end due to the stock shortfall.
Dealers said prices had risen due to an anticipated shortage of coffee in the remaining three months of 1996.
Growers said unseasonal rains had reduced India's projected coffee output in 1995/96 (October-September) to about 160,000 tonnes, against the Coffee Board's target of 235,000 tonnes.

Coffee Board member H.B. Jayaprasad said growers did not have much coffee with them. "The harvest has been bought by the dealers. If most of it is exported, they are responsible for not covering the domestic requirement for six months," he said.
"Stocks now are the lowest. There is no indication of fresh arrival of the beans till November," said A. Rajagopal, a wholesale dealer.
